lesson_title: Twenty-Five Cuts to a Single Atom
hook_text: Take a cube of gold and keep cutting it in half. After only about twenty-five cuts, the next piece would not be gold any more.
clip_script: A cube of gold, one centimetre on each side. Cut it in half. Still gold. Again. Still gold. A Greek thinker called Democritus guessed, around 2 400 years ago, that you could not do this for ever; eventually you would reach a piece that cannot be cut. He called it atomos, uncuttable. In 1803 John Dalton turned that guess into science, with measurements. And the numbers are wild. One gold atom is about 0.29 billionths of a metre across, so it takes only about twenty-five halvings to get from your cube to a single atom; each cut halves the size, and twenty-five halvings shrink it more than thirty million times. A full stop is about five million atoms wide. And here is the twist: there are only about ninety natural kinds of atom, yet they build everything, like twenty-six letters building every word in the dictionary. Your body is mostly four letters: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen.
visual_style: A whiteboard gold cube splitting in half repeatedly with a counter climbing to 25, then a single circle labelled Au; then the alphabet with atom symbols replacing letters.
pacing: Rhythmic cutting with a ticking counter, a pause at the single atom, a quick finish on the alphabet.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and see how ninety letters write the whole world.
